headline: Drawing is visual thinking—the most direct connection between mind and mark
universal_truth: The simplest tools are often the most powerful; constraints focus creativity
fun_facts: Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks contain over 13,000 pages of drawings—his way of thinking
Children draw naturally, but most adults stop—losing a universal human ability
Architects, scientists, and inventors draw to think, not just to communicate
discussion_questions: Why do most adults stop drawing?
How is drawing a form of thinking?
What could you understand better by drawing it?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: A pencil and paper—the simplest tools—can capture anything you can imagine. Drawing is the most direct connection between thought and visible mark. Before writing, before computers, humans drew to record, plan, and understand.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Most children draw constantly. Most adults have stopped. What happens to this natural human ability, and why does it matter?

options.text: We become self-critical about 'talent' and stop practicing—but drawing is a skill, not a gift
options.response: Yes. Around age 10, we become embarrassed by 'bad' drawings and stop. But drawing is learnable—those who continue, improve. We quit just as we could progress.

options.text: Adults have other ways to express themselves and don't need drawing
options.response: We have other tools, but drawing offers unique thinking capabilities we lose...

q1.title: Visual Thinking
q1.script: Drawing isn't just recording—it's thinking. When you draw something, you understand it differently than when you look at it. The act of translating observation to mark changes perception. Artists see more because they draw.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Visual Thinking"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Leonardo's Method
q2.script: Leonardo da Vinci filled 13,000 pages with drawings—anatomy, machines, water, ideas. For him, drawing was how he thought. The sketches weren't preparation for 'real' work; they were the work of understanding.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Simple Power
q3.script: A pencil costs almost nothing. Paper is everywhere. Yet with these simple tools, you can design buildings, plan surgeries, imagine machines, or express emotions. Constraints don't limit creativity—they focus it.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: The simplest tools are often the most powerful. Drawing teaches that constraints focus creativity. You don't need expensive equipment to think visually—you need practice and permission.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 156. Tomorrow, we'll discover why every culture dances. Until then, draw something—anything. Give yourself permission to think with lines.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Drawing Practice - Think With Lines
growTrack.learning_objective: Reclaim drawing as a thinking tool
growTrack.activity: Draw something today—anything. Not to create art, but to see differently. Draw your coffee cup, your hand, a problem you're solving. Notice what you see while drawing that you didn't see before. Drawing is thinking.
